title: BE one-shot: the end-term in one go
intro_md:
Everything Athena has for the Business Economics end-term, in the order that wins marks: **market structures and monopoly numericals first**, then **industry concentration** and **specialized investments** (together these were most of the 2025 end-term), then **production and cost**, **demand forecasting**, and a fast revision of the **mid-term topics**.

Each part gives you the idea in one line, a picture, a worked example from the slides, practice from the slides and past papers, and the exact way to write the answer. Pick your hours, follow the plan from the top, and tick each part when it feels solid.
paper_md:
**The 2025 end-term:** 40 marks, 120 minutes, all questions compulsory, calculators allowed.

- **Q1: five short questions × 4 marks = 20 marks** (explain, compare, one small calculation).
- **Q2 to Q5: four questions × 5 marks = 20 marks** (a cost function, profit-maximizing output and price, a theory question with a diagram).

sections.title: Monopoly: profit-maximizing output, price and profit
sections.why: The 2025 end-term Q3 and Q4 (5 marks each) were both monopoly numericals: find Q where MR = MC, read P from demand, then profit.
sections.big_idea: A monopolist picks the quantity where MR = MC, then charges the highest price buyers will pay for that quantity.
sections.body_md:
**Marginal revenue and profit maximization.** A monopoly can charge more than MC, but **not anything it likes\**: the higher the price, the less it sells.

To sell one more unit it must **lower the price on every unit\**, so **MR is below the demand curve\**. For a straight-line demand **P = a - bQ\**, MR has the same start but **twice the slope\**: **MR = a - 2bQ\**.

MR and elasticity are linked: where demand is **elastic\** MR is positive and revenue rises; at **unit elastic\** MR = 0 and **total revenue is highest\**; where **inelastic\**, MR is negative.

**The two-step rule:**

1. Find the output where **MR = MC\**.
2. Go **up to the demand curve\** to read the price.

Profit = **(P - ATC) x Q**.

**Worked example: P = 10 - Q.** This is the slide's example, drawn below with its own numbers. Notice how the profit box sits between the price **$6** and average cost at 4 units.

visuals.title: Demand and marginal revenue
visuals.caption: MR starts at the same price as demand but falls twice as fast. Above the midpoint demand is elastic; at the midpoint MR = 0 and total revenue peaks; below it demand is inelastic.

visuals.caption: MR = MC at Q = 4. Up to demand: P = $6. Average cost at 4 units is 3.5, so profit is (6 - 3.5) x 4 = $10.

sections.title: Perfect competition vs monopolistic competition
sections.why: The 2025 end-term Q1(e) (4 marks) asked to compare the market environments of perfect competition and monopolistic competition with examples.
sections.big_idea: When thousands of firms sell the exact same thing, no single firm can choose its price: it takes the market price.
sections.body_md:
**The environment and its implications.** Picture a vegetable market where every stall sells identical tomatoes and every buyer can see every price. If one seller charges more, buyers simply walk to the next stall.

That is **perfect competition\**: **many buyers and sellers\**, an **identical product\**, **perfect information\**, **no transaction costs\** and **free entry and exit\**.

Three things follow:

- Each firm is a **price taker\**, so the price it gets for one more unit is the market price: **P = MR\**.
- In the **short run\** a firm can make a **profit or a loss\**.
- In the **long run\**, entry and exit push **profit to zero\**.

Why study something so rare? It is the **benchmark\** every other market is compared with, and it shows managers why **differentiation\** matters.

**Environment and limited market power.** Think of shampoo brands. There are **numerous sellers\**, and each brand is a little **different\**, so each firm faces a **downward sloping demand curve\**: it can raise its price a bit without losing every customer.

But the brands are **close substitutes\**, so buyers do switch. That makes each firm's demand **more elastic\** than a monopolist's. Add **free entry and exit\**, and the firm has only **limited market power\**.

Like a monopolist, it can price **above MC\**, and its MR lies below its demand curve.

**Short run and long run.** **Short run:** produce where **MR = MC\** and charge the price on the demand curve, exactly like a monopolist. If that price is above ATC, the brand **makes a profit\**.

**Long run:** profit attracts rivals. Their **new brands steal market share\**, so your demand curve **shifts left\** (D to D1). This continues until the demand curve just **touches the AC curve\**: there **P = AC\** and **profit is zero\**.

**The good, the bad and the ugly.** | For | Verdict |
|---|---|
| **Consumers (good)** | Product variety |
| **Society (bad)** | P > MC, excess capacity, unexploited economies of scale |
| **Managers (ugly)** | P = ATC > minimum average cost, and zero profits in the long run |

sections.title: Industry concentration: C4 and HHI
sections.why: The 2025 end-term Q1(c) (4 marks) gave three firms' sales and asked for the HHI.
sections.big_idea: C4 adds the top four firms' shares; HHI squares every firm's share, adds them up and multiplies by 10,000.
sections.body_md:
**Two measures of concentration.** Both measure **how much of the market a few firms control**.

**C4** (four-firm concentration ratio): add the market shares of the **four biggest** firms. Market share wi = Si / ST (firm's sales over total industry sales).

**HHI** (Herfindahl-Hirschman Index): square **every** firm's share, add them, multiply by **10,000**.

Why square? Squaring makes **big firms count much more**: a 50% firm adds 2,500, but five 10% firms add only 500 together. So HHI rises sharply when one firm dominates.

**Worked example: five banks.** This is the slide's example, and last year's paper asked the same kind of question with three firms, worked below.

**Integration and the merger guidelines.** The **DOJ/FTC Horizontal Merger Guidelines** use HHI. A merger **may be challenged** if **both** hold:

1. HHI **exceeds 1800** (or would after the merger), **and**
2. the merger **raises HHI by more than 100**.

But the guidelines also accept that mergers can bring **efficiencies** that lower prices, and in most cases they let firms merge.

sides.title: Horizontal

watch_out: Use shares as **decimals** (0.2, not 20) before squaring, then multiply by 10,000.
C4 uses only the **top four**; HHI uses **all** firms.
Do not forget to divide by total sales first. Squaring raw sales (10², 30²) gives the wrong answer.
Both conditions are needed: above 1800 **and** an increase of more than 100.
sections.memory_trick: **C4: add four. HHI: square all, add, times 10,000.**
sections.exam_answer_md:
**C4** = w1 + w2 + w3 + w4, the sum of the market shares of the top four firms, where wi = Si/ST. **HHI** = 10,000 x sum of wi², the sum of the squared market shares of all firms in the industry, multiplied by 10,000.

Five banks at 20 percent each: **C4** = 0.2 + 0.2 + 0.2 + 0.2 = **0.8**; **HHI** = 10,000 x (5 x 0.2²) = **2,000**.

Three firms with sales 10, 10 and 30: shares 0.2, 0.2, 0.6; HHI = 10,000 x (0.04 + 0.04 + 0.36) = **4,400**.

**Vertical integration:** various stages in the production of a single product carried out by one firm. **Horizontal integration:** merging the production of similar products into a single firm. **Conglomerate merger:** integrating different product lines into a single firm. Under the horizontal merger guidelines, a merger may be challenged if HHI exceeds 1800 (or would after the merger) and the merger increases HHI by more than 100, though efficiencies are recognized.

sections.title: Rothschild index, Lerner index and Dansby-Willig index
sections.why: The 2025 end-term Q1(d) (4 marks) asked to explain the Rothschild Index and Dansby-Willig Index with their applications.
sections.big_idea: The Rothschild index compares how sensitive the whole market is to price with how sensitive one firm is: near 0 is competition, 1 is monopoly.
sections.body_md:
**The Rothschild index.** **R = ET / EF**

- **ET**: elasticity of demand for the **total market**.
- **EF**: elasticity of demand for **one firm's** product.

If there are many similar firms, raising **your** price sends buyers to rivals, so **EF is large** and R is **close to 0** (perfect competition). If you are the only firm, your demand **is** the market demand, so EF = ET and **R = 1** (monopoly).

**Application:** it tells a manager how much pricing power firms in the industry have. In the slide's table, Tobacco and Chemicals have R = 1.00; Food is only 0.26.

**Performance and the Dansby-Willig index.** **Performance** is the **profits and social welfare** an industry produces.

**Social welfare = CS + PS** (consumer surplus plus producer surplus).

The **Dansby-Willig Performance Index** measures **by how much social welfare would improve** if firms in the industry **expanded output in a socially efficient manner**. A **higher** number means more welfare is being left on the table, so the industry is performing **worse** for society.

**Application:** regulators can use it to see which industries would gain most from more output. In the slide's table Chemicals (0.67) has the most room to improve and Textiles (0.38) the least.

**The Lerner index.** **L = (P - MC) / P**

If a firm charges exactly its marginal cost, L = 0: it has **no market power**. The higher the markup, the closer L gets to **1**, meaning **weak price competition** and **market power**.

**From Lerner index to markup factor.** Rearranging L = (P - MC) / P gives **P = [1 / (1 - L)] x MC**. The **markup factor** is **1/(1 - L)**.

- L = 0: markup factor 1, so **P = MC**.
- L = 0.20: markup factor **1/0.80 = 1.25**, so price is **1.25 times MC**.

In the slide's table, Tobacco has L = 0.76 and a markup factor of 4.17.
watch_out: Market elasticity goes on **top**: R = ET / EF.
R = 1 means **monopoly**, R near 0 means **perfect competition**.
A **higher** Dansby-Willig number means **more** room to improve welfare, not better performance.
Divide by **P**, not by MC.
sections.memory_trick: **Total over firm.**
sections.exam_answer_md:
The **Rothschild Index** measures the elasticity of industry demand relative to that of an individual firm: **R = ET / EF**. It lies between 0 (perfect competition) and 1 (monopoly); with many firms producing similar products it is close to zero. **Application:** it measures the market power of firms in an industry, e.g. Tobacco and Chemicals 1.00, Food 0.26.

**Performance** refers to the profits and social welfare that result in an industry; social welfare = CS + PS. The **Dansby-Willig Performance Index** measures by how much social welfare would improve if firms in an industry expanded output in a socially efficient manner. **Application:** it identifies industries where more output would raise welfare most (e.g. Chemicals 0.67 vs Textiles 0.38).

The **Lerner Index** L = (P - MC) / P measures the difference between price and marginal cost as a fraction of price. It ranges from 0 to 1. When P = MC it is zero and the firm has no market power; closer to 1 indicates weak price competition and market power.

Rearranging the Lerner index: P = [1/(1 - L)] x MC, so the **markup factor is 1/(1 - L)**. When L = 0 the markup factor is 1 and P = MC; when L = 0.20 the markup factor is 1.25.

sections.title: Specialized investments and contract length
sections.why: The 2025 end-term Q1(b) (4 marks) asked to examine the impact of specialized investments on contract length with examples.
sections.big_idea: A specialized investment is one that is worthless outside this one deal, which makes both sides nervous.
sections.body_md:
**What specialized investments are.** Imagine a supplier who builds a factory **right next to** your plant, or buys a machine that only makes **your** part. If you walk away, that investment is almost useless.

That is a **specialized investment**: it allows the two parties to exchange but has **little or no value outside the relationship**.

Because one side is now locked in, these investments **raise transaction costs**: **costly bargaining**, **underinvestment** (nobody wants to be the one stuck) and **opportunism and the hold-up problem**.

**Contract length: marginal benefit meets marginal cost.** How long should a contract be? Where the **marginal benefit** of one more year equals its **marginal cost**.

- A **longer** contract protects specialized investments from hold-up, so when specialized investments matter more, the **MB curve shifts out** and the contract gets **longer**.
- A **longer** contract is harder to write when the future is complicated, so a **more complex contracting environment** shifts **MC up** and the contract gets **shorter**. A **simpler** environment does the opposite.

**Choosing the method: the decision tree.** Follow the tree from the top.

- If there are **no substantial specialized investments**, nobody can be held up, so just use the **spot market**.
- If there **are**, you need protection. If writing a contract is **not** too complex compared with the cost of integrating, use a **contract**.
- If it **is** too complex, **make the input yourself** (vertical integration).

visuals.title: More specialized investment: MB shifts out, contract gets longer
visuals.caption: The need for specialized investments raises the benefit of a longer contract: MB0 moves to MB1 and optimal length rises from L0 to L1.

visuals.title: More complex contracting: MC shifts up, contract gets shorter
visuals.caption: A more complex environment raises the cost of each extra year: MC0 moves up to MC2 and optimal length falls from L0 to L2.

nodes.label: Substantial specialized investments relative to contracting costs?
Complex contracting environment relative to costs of integration?

watch_out: List all **four** types in the exam: site, physical-asset, dedicated assets, human capital.
Specialized investments move the **MB** curve; complexity moves the **MC** curve. Do not swap them.
Less complex contracting shifts MC **down**, so contracts get **longer**.
Spot exchange is the answer only when specialized investments are **not** substantial.
sections.memory_trick: **Site, stuff, staff**: where it is (site), the machine (physical asset, dedicated assets), the people (human capital).
sections.exam_answer_md:
**Specialized investments** are investments made to allow two parties to exchange but which have little or no value outside the exchange relationship. Types: site specificity, physical-asset specificity, dedicated assets, human capital. They lead to higher transaction costs through costly bargaining, underinvestment, and opportunism and the hold-up problem.

The optimal contract length is where the marginal benefit (MB) of extending the contract equals its marginal cost (MC).

- **Greater need for specialized investments** raises MB (MB0 to MB1): **longer contract** (L0 to L1). Example: a supplier building a plant next to the buyer wants a long contract.
- **More complex contracting environment** raises MC (MC0 to MC2): **shorter contract** (L0 to L2).
- **Less complex environment** lowers MC (MC0 to MC1): **longer contract**.

(Draw the two graphs with contract length on the x-axis.)

Optimal input procurement: if specialized investments are not substantial relative to contracting costs, use **spot exchange**. If they are, and the contracting environment is not complex relative to the costs of integration, use a **contract**; if it is complex, use **vertical integration**. The optimal method depends on the nature of transaction costs and the specialized nature of the inputs.

sections.title: Production functions: linear, Leontief, Cobb-Douglas
sections.why: The end-term is built on production and cost (the 2025 end-term was almost all Unit IV and V). The professor's two worked questions here are ready-made short numericals.
sections.big_idea: A production function tells you the most output you can make from given amounts of capital (K) and labour (L): Q = F(K, L).
sections.body_md:
**Production function: Q = F(K, L)**, the **maximum** amount of output that can be produced with K units of capital and L units of labour.

- **Short run:** some inputs are **fixed**. **Long run:** all inputs are **variable**.

**Three forms you must know:**

| Form | Formula | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| **Linear** | Q = aK + bL | Inputs are **perfect substitutes** |
| **Leontief** | Q = min{bK, cL} | Inputs are used in **fixed proportions** |
| **Cobb-Douglas** | Q = K^a L^b | Inputs have a **degree of substitutability** |

**Measuring productivity:**

- **Total product (TP):** the maximum output from the inputs.
- **Average product:** APL = Q/L, the output of an 'average' worker (APK = Q/K for capital).
- **Marginal product:** MPL = ΔQ/ΔL, the output produced by the **last** worker. It is the slope of the production function.

sections.exam_answer_md:
**Production function:** Q = F(K, L), the maximum output that can be produced with K units of capital and L units of labour.

- **Linear:** Q = aK + bL, inputs are perfect substitutes.
- **Leontief:** Q = min{bK, cL}, inputs are used in fixed proportions.
- **Cobb-Douglas:** Q = K^a L^b, inputs have a degree of substitutability.

Example: Q = min{3K, 4L} with K = 5, L = 2 gives 3K = 15, 4L = 8, so **Q = min{15, 8} = 8**.

sections.title: TP, AP, MP and the law of variable proportions
sections.why: A TP table turned into AP and MP is a quick numerical, and the law of variable proportions is a classic 'Explain with a diagram' question. The professor solved this exact table in class.
sections.big_idea: Add workers to a fixed factory and each new worker first adds more output, then less, and in the end can even reduce it.
sections.body_md:
**Law of Variable Proportions** (short run): as successive units of a **variable input** are added to a **fixed input**, the **marginal product** of the variable input **first increases, reaches a maximum, and eventually decreases**.

**Why it rises first:** the fixed input is **underutilised**. More workers allow **specialisation**, better **coordination** and **better utilisation** of the machines and space.

**Why it falls later:** the fixed input becomes a **constraint**. Workers **wait for machines**, the space becomes **crowded**, and the chances for more specialisation are **exhausted**.

The three stages: **increasing**, **diminishing** and **negative** marginal returns.

**How much labour to hire?** Hire labour until the **value of marginal product equals the wage**: **VMPL = w**, where **VMPL = P × MPL**. For capital: VMPK = r.

**Law of Variable Proportions:** as successive units of a variable input are added to a fixed input, the marginal product of the variable input first increases, reaches a maximum, and eventually decreases.

sections.title: Isoquants, isocosts and cost minimization
sections.why: The 2025 end-term asked exactly this for 4 marks: 'Utilizing the iso-quant and iso-cost curves explain the cost minimization principle'. The diagram is half the marks.
sections.big_idea: The cheapest way to make a given output is where the isoquant just touches the lowest isocost line: there MRTS = w/r.
sections.body_md:
**Isoquant:** the long-run combinations of K and L that give the **same output**. Its shape shows how easily one input can replace the other.

**MRTS** (marginal rate of technical substitution): the rate at which two inputs are substituted while keeping the same output. **MRTS_KL = MPL / MPK**.

| Isoquant | Production function | Shape and substitution |
|---|---|---|
| Linear | Q = aK + bL | Straight line; perfect substitutes; MRTS = b/a, constant |
| Leontief | Q = min{bK, cL} | Fixed proportions; perfect complements; no substitution |
| Cobb-Douglas | Q = K^a L^b | Curved; diminishing MRTS |

**Isocost:** all input combinations that **cost the same**: **wL + rK = C**, or **K = (1/r)C - (w/r)L**. Isocosts farther from the origin cost more. A change in input prices changes the **slope**.

**Cost minimization:** marginal product per dollar spent should be equal for all inputs:

**MPL / w = MPK / r**, which is the same as **MPL / MPK = w / r**, which is just **MRTS_KL = w / r**.

On the graph this is where the **slope of the isocost = slope of the isoquant**.

**If the wage falls** (w0 to w1), the isocost rotates. To make the same output Q0 the firm moves to a **lower isocost** at point B, using **more labour and less capital**.

visuals.title: When the wage falls: A to B
visuals.caption: A cheaper wage makes the isocost flatter. The same output Q0 is now made at B on the lower isocost C1: more labour (L0 to L1), less capital (K0 to K1).

watch_out: Cost minimization is a **tangency** (the lines just touch). If an isocost **cuts** the isoquant, a cheaper isocost can still reach that output.
Keep labour on top on both sides: **MPL/MPK = w/r**.

sections.exam_answer_md:
**Isoquant:** combinations of K and L that give the same level of output. **Isocost:** combinations of inputs with the same cost, **wL + rK = C**.

**Cost minimization principle:** a given output is produced at the lowest cost where the isocost line is **tangent** to the isoquant, so the slope of the isocost equals the slope of the isoquant:

**MPL / w = MPK / r**, that is, **MRTS_KL = MPL / MPK = w / r**.

Marginal product per dollar spent is then equal for all inputs; any other point on the isoquant lies on a higher isocost.

(Draw: K on the vertical axis, L on the horizontal, a curved isoquant, three isocost lines, and mark the tangency point.)

If the wage falls, the isocost becomes flatter and the firm substitutes labour for capital (point A to point B).

sections.big_idea: Total cost = fixed cost + variable cost. Divide by Q for the averages; the change in total cost from one more unit is marginal cost.
sections.body_md:
**Short run:** fixed costs (FC), sunk costs, variable costs (VC), total costs (TC). **Long run:** all costs are variable; no fixed costs.

- **FC:** costs that **do not change** as output changes.
- **VC(Q):** costs that **vary** with output.
- **C(Q) = VC(Q) + FC**
- **Sunk cost:** a cost that is forever lost after it has been paid. Decision makers should **ignore sunk costs**.

| Measure | Formula |
|---|---|
| Average fixed cost | AFC = FC/Q |
| Average variable cost | AVC = VC(Q)/Q |
| Average total cost | ATC = C(Q)/Q = AVC + AFC |
| Marginal cost | MC = ΔC/ΔQ |

**Shapes:** AFC keeps **falling**. AVC and ATC are **U-shaped**. **MC cuts AVC and ATC at their minimum points.**

sections.title: Demand forecasting: meaning, steps and methods
sections.why: Demand forecasting is a whole syllabus unit; its theory gives easy 'Explain' marks (the steps, qualitative versus quantitative, choosing a model).
sections.big_idea: Demand forecasting estimates future demand from past data, market information and judgement; it is a bridge between an uncertain future and today's decisions.
sections.body_md:
**Demand forecasting:** the process of estimating the future demand for a product or service using **historical data**, **market information**, and/or **statistical and judgmental methods**.

**Decisions that need forecasts:** which markets to pursue, what products to produce, how many people to hire, how many inputs to purchase, how many units to produce.

**What forecasts are like:** they are **rarely perfect**; more accurate for **aggregated** data than for individual items; more accurate for **shorter** than longer periods.

**Two families of methods:**

- **Qualitative:** generated subjectively by the forecaster: market research and consumer surveys; the **Delphi method** (consensus among a group of experts).
- **Quantitative (statistical):** mathematical models. **Time series** models assume the future follows past patterns; **causal** models explore cause and effect with leading indicators (housing starts and appliance sales).

**Time series data = historic pattern + random variation.** The pattern may include **level, trend, seasonality and cycle**.

**Choosing a model:** the amount and type of data, the degree of accuracy required, the length of the forecast horizon, and the patterns in the data.

**Methods:** qualitative (market research and consumer surveys, the Delphi method) and quantitative (time series: trend, moving average, exponential smoothing; causal models with leading indicators).

sections.title: Moving averages and choosing a method with RMSE
sections.why: Moving averages and RMSE are at the heart of the forecasting numericals; the professor's practice question asks for both methods and an RMSE comparison.
sections.big_idea: A moving average forecasts the next period as the average of the last few actual values; compare methods with RMSE and pick the lower one.
sections.body_md:
Data contains an underlying pattern and random fluctuations. A trend line forces one shape onto the data; a **moving average** simply **smooths** it by averaging recent observations.

**3-period moving average:** **F(t+1) = (Y(t) + Y(t-1) + Y(t-2)) / 3**

Why use it: it **smoothens random fluctuations**, is **easy to calculate**, and **uses recent observations**.

**3-period or 5-period?** Calculate the **Root Mean Square Error** for each and choose the **lower** one:

**RMSE = √[ Σ(At - Ft)² / n ]**, where n = the number of periods for which forecasts are available.

On the slide: RMSE(3) = √(2416.367/6) = **20.068** and RMSE(5) = √(2866/4) = **26.767**, so the **3-year moving average** is preferred and the forecast for 2026 is **140**.

sections.big_idea: Exponential smoothing: next forecast = α × this period's actual + (1 - α) × this period's forecast, so recent data counts more.
sections.body_md:
A moving average gives **equal importance** to every value in its window. But this year's sales usually say more about next year than older sales do. **Exponential smoothing** gives **more importance to recent observations** and progressively less to older ones.

**F(t+1) = αY(t) + (1 - α)F(t)**, with **0 < α < 1**

- F(t+1) = forecast for the next period
- Y(t) = actual value in the current period
- F(t) = forecast for the current period
- α = the smoothing constant (a question may call it w)

**You need a starting forecast.** The slides use the **first actual observation**; the 2025 mid-term said to use the **average**. Use whatever the question says.

sections.title: Perfect competition: P = MC, shutdown and the long run
sections.why: Market structures carried most of the 2025 end-term; the price-taker rule and shutdown rule are the base for every comparison.
sections.big_idea: A price taker keeps producing until the cost of one more unit (MC) rises to the price it gets.
sections.body_md:
**Setting price and output.** The **market\** sets the price where supply meets demand. The single firm sees a **flat demand line\** at that price: it can sell as much as it likes at Pe, and nothing above it.

Every firm maximizes profit where **MR = MC\**. For a price taker MR is the price, so the rule becomes **P = MC\**.

On the graph, follow the price line across until it hits the **MC\** curve. Drop down: that is the best output **Qf\***. The **profit\** is the box between the price and **ATC\** at that output: **(Pe - ATC) x Qf\***.

**Worked example: P = $10.** This is the slide's own numerical example, and it is exactly the kind of question the paper asks.

The recipe never changes: **find MC, set it equal to the price, solve for Q, then profit = revenue - cost\**.

**Losses and the shutdown rule.** Sometimes the price falls below **ATC\**: the firm makes a **loss\**. Should it close?

If it closes, it still has to pay its **fixed costs\** (rent, machines), so it loses all of them. If it keeps operating and the price covers its **variable costs\**, every unit also chips in a little towards the fixed costs. So operating loses **less\**.

**The rule:**

- **Keep operating\** while **P ≥ min AVC\**.
- **Shut down\** when **P < min AVC\**.

That is why the firm's **short-run supply curve\** is just its **MC curve above minimum AVC\**.

**Entry in the long run.** If firms are making profit and anyone can enter, new firms **pour in\**. This chain follows:

1. Entry **shifts market supply right\** (S to S\*).
2. The **market price falls\** (Pe to Pe\*).
3. Each firm's flat demand line **drops\** (Df to Df\*).
4. Each firm **cuts output\** to where the new price meets MC.
5. Entry stops only when **profit is zero\**.

At that point three things are true: **P = MC\** (socially efficient output), **P = minimum AC\** (efficient plant size) and **zero profit\** (firms earn just enough to cover their opportunity cost).

If there are **barriers to entry\**, this never happens and profits **persist\**.

A perfectly competitive firm maximizes profit where **MR = MC\**. Since **MR = P**, it sets **P = MC\**.

Profit = **(Pe - ATC) x Qf\***. (Draw the market graph setting Pe, and the firm's graph with MC, ATC, AVC, the flat line Pe = Df = MR, and shade the profit box.)

A firm should continue to operate (sustain short-run losses) if its operating loss is less than its fixed costs.

**Shut down when P < min AVC; continue while P ≥ min AVC.** Hence the firm's short-run supply curve is its **MC curve above minimum AVC\**. (Draw MC, ATC, AVC with Pe between min AVC and ATC, and shade the loss.)

Short-run profits lead to entry. Entry increases market supply, drives down the market price and increases market quantity. Each firm's demand shifts down, so it reduces output. **Long-run profits are zero.**

sections.title: Monopoly power and deadweight loss
sections.why: A theory question with a diagram is likely: sources of monopoly power and why governments dislike monopoly.
sections.big_idea: A monopoly is the only seller in its market, and its power comes either from cost advantages or from legal and contract barriers.
sections.body_md:
**The monopoly environment and its sources.** A **monopoly\** is a **single firm serving the relevant market\**. Most real monopolies are **local\**: the only cinema in a small town.

Because it is the only seller, **its demand curve is the market demand curve\**. It controls the price, but a higher price means it sells less.

Where does the power come from?

**Long run, deadweight loss and the case for monopoly.** In the long run a monopoly **keeps its profit\**: nothing changes **unless the source of its power is removed\**.

Governments dislike this because **P > MC\**: some buyers would happily pay more than it costs to make another unit, but the monopolist doesn't sell to them. Output is **too low\** and the price **too high\**. The value of those missing trades is the **deadweight loss of monopoly\**.

In the slide's example, a competitive market would produce where demand meets MC (Q = 8), but the monopolist stops at 4.

**The other side:** economies of scale, scope and cost complementarities can make a monopoly cheap enough to outweigh the harm, and monopoly profits **encourage innovation\**.

**Two plants:** a monopoly with two factories sets **MR = MC1 = MC2**, and charges the price for the total Q = Q1 + Q2.

visuals.title: Deadweight loss of monopoly
visuals.caption: The monopolist stops at 4 units where MR = MC. Between 4 and 8 units buyers value the good above MC, but those units are never made: the shaded triangle is the deadweight loss.

watch_out: Patents are a **created** source, not a natural one.
The deadweight loss triangle runs from **QM** out to where **demand meets MC**, not to where MR meets MC.
sections.memory_trick: **Natural = cheaper to be big. Created = the law or a contract keeps others out.**
sections.exam_answer_md:
A monopoly is a single firm serving the relevant market; its demand is the market demand curve.

**Natural sources:** economies of scale, economies of scope, cost complementarities. **Created sources:** patents and other legal barriers (like licenses), tying contracts, exclusive contracts.

Under monopoly **P > MC\**: too little output at too high a price, creating a **deadweight loss\**. No long-run adjustment occurs unless the source of monopoly power is eliminated.

**Arguments for monopoly:** economies of scale, scope and cost complementarities may outweigh the negative effects of market power; it encourages innovation. **Multi-plant rule:** MR(Q) = MC1(Q1) = MC2(Q2), with P = P(Q), Q = Q1 + Q2. (Draw D, MR, MC and shade the deadweight-loss triangle.)

sections.title: One cost function, three market structures
sections.why: The slides' synthesizing example ties the whole session together in one numerical.
sections.big_idea: Same cost function, but as a price taker at $40 the firm loses $25.
sections.body_md:
**The set-up and the price taker.** One cost function, **C(Q) = 125 + 4Q²**, worked under three market structures. MC is the same in every case, **MC = 8Q\**, because cost does not depend on the market.

First case: you are a **price taker\** and the market price is **$40**.

**Monopoly or monopolistic competition.** Facing **P = 100 - Q**:

- **MR = 100 - 2Q**; set 100 - 2Q = 8Q, so **Q = 10**
- **P = 100 - 10 = $90**
- Profit = (90)(10) - (125 + 4(100)) = **$375**

**Implications:** a **monopolist** will not face entry unless patents or other barriers are removed. A **monopolistically competitive** firm should expect others to **clone** its product, so **profits decline over time**.

worked.question_md: C(Q) = 125 + 4Q². You are a price taker and other firms charge $40. Find output, profit and the implication.

steps.why: A price taker sets P = MC.

sections.title: Procuring inputs and the principal-agent problem
sections.why: The rest of Session 10: spot exchange, contracts, vertical integration, transaction costs and incentives.
sections.big_idea: A firm can buy an input once, sign a contract for it, or make it itself.
sections.body_md:
**Three ways to get inputs.** Think of a car maker that needs seats.

- **Spot exchange**: buy seats from whoever is selling today, then part ways.
- **Contract**: sign a legal agreement with one seat supplier for, say, three years.
- **Vertical integration**: stop buying seats and **make them in-house**.

The rest of the session is about **which one to choose**.

**Strengths and weaknesses of each method.** Every method trades something off.

**Hold-up** means that once you depend on one supplier, they can suddenly demand a higher price because you have nowhere else to go.

**Opportunism** is the general version: one side taking advantage of the other.

**Transaction costs.** The price on the invoice is not the whole cost. You also spend money and time **searching** for a supplier, **negotiating** the deal, and on **other investments** the deal needs.

Some deals are **general** (anyone could supply you). Others are **specific** to one trading relationship, and those are the ones that cause trouble, as the next topic shows.

**What the problem is.** The **principal** is the one who hires; the **agent** is the one who does the work.

- **Shareholders** (principal) cannot watch the **manager** (agent) all day.
- A **manager** (principal) cannot watch every **worker** (agent).

So when profits fall, was it **low effort** or **bad luck**? The principal cannot tell. That is the **principal-agent problem**, and the fix is to **align the agent's interests** with the principal's.

**The fixes.** A manager who holds **stock options** gains when the share price rises, just like the shareholders. A worker on **piece rates** earns more for every unit made. That is what aligning interests means.

Outside pressure helps too: a manager who does badly risks their **reputation**, and a badly run firm can be **taken over**.

Both contracts and vertical integration **reduce opportunism**; only spot exchange risks hold-up.
The price paid to the supplier is **not** a transaction cost; it is everything over and above it.

sections.exam_answer_md:
**Spot exchange:** the buyer and seller of an input meet, exchange, and then go their separate ways. **Contract:** a legal document that creates an extended relationship between a buyer and a seller. **Vertical integration:** a firm shuns other suppliers and chooses to produce an input internally.

**Spot exchange:** specialization, avoids contracting costs and the costs of vertical integration; but possible hold-up problem. **Contracting:** specialization, reduces opportunism, avoids skimping on specialized investments; but costly in complex environments. **Vertical integration:** reduces opportunism, avoids contracting costs; but lost specialization and may increase organizational costs.

**Transaction costs** are the costs of acquiring an input over and above the amount paid to the input supplier. They include search costs, negotiation costs and other required investments or expenditures. Some transactions are general in nature, while others are specific to a trading relationship.

The **principal-agent problem** occurs when the principal cannot observe the effort of the agent (shareholders and managers; managers and workers). The principal cannot determine whether a bad outcome was the result of the agent's low effort or bad luck, so principals must devise plans to align the agents' interests with their own.

**Owners and managers:** internal incentives (incentive contracts, stock options, year-end bonuses) and external incentives (personal reputation, potential for takeover). **Managers and workers:** profit sharing, revenue sharing, piece rates, time clocks and spot checks.

sections.title: Structure, conduct, performance
sections.why: The framing of Session 11; useful as an introduction to any industry question.
sections.big_idea: To understand an industry, look at how it is built (structure), how firms behave (conduct) and how well it does (performance).
sections.body_md:
**Structure, conduct and performance.** Economists study an industry in three layers:

- **Structure** is the shape of the market: how many firms and how big, how **concentrated**, the technology and costs, demand, and how easy it is to **enter or exit**.
- **Conduct** is what firms **do**: pricing, advertising, R&D, mergers.
- **Performance** is the **result**: profitability and social welfare.

**The SCP paradigm and the feedback critique.** The **SCP paradigm** takes a **causal view**: structure decides conduct, and conduct decides performance, in one direction.

The **feedback critique** says it is not one-way. A firm's **conduct** (say, a merger or heavy advertising) can **change the structure**. And **performance** (big profits) can change both conduct and structure, for example by attracting entrants.

The modern approach looks at all three **together**.

**Five forces, technology and barriers to entry.** The **five forces** connect to SCP by explaining the **level, growth and sustainability of industry profits**:

1. **Entry** (entry costs, sunk costs, economies of scale, network effects, reputation, switching costs)
2. **Power of input suppliers**
3. **Power of buyers**
4. **Industry rivalry**
5. **Substitutes and complements**

**Barriers to entry** on the slides: **capital requirements**, **patents and copyrights**, **economies of scale**, **economies of scope**.

Industries also differ in **technology**: some are **labor intensive**, some **capital intensive**, others use both.

steps.label: Conduct
steps.note: shapes performance, and can change structure

watch_out: Mergers are **conduct** (something firms do), even though they change structure.
Say clearly that the feedback critique means **no one-way causal link**.
Barriers to entry list: capital, patents and copyrights, economies of **scale** and of **scope**. Do not add things that are not on the slide.
sections.memory_trick: **Built, behave, result.**
sections.exam_answer_md:
**Market structure:** number and size of firms, industry concentration, technological and cost conditions, demand conditions, ease of entry and exit. **Conduct:** pricing, advertising, R&D, merger activity. **Performance:** profitability, social welfare.

The **Structure-Conduct-Performance paradigm** holds a causal view: market structure determines conduct, which determines performance. The **feedback critique** argues there is no one-way causal link: conduct can affect market structure, and market performance can affect conduct as well as market structure.

The five forces (entry, power of input suppliers, power of buyers, industry rivalry, substitutes and complements) determine the level, growth and sustainability of industry profits. Barriers to entry include capital requirements, patents and copyrights, economies of scale and economies of scope.

sections.title: Long-run cost: economies of scale and scope
sections.why: A favourite 'Explain' question: why the long-run average cost curve is U-shaped, plus economies of scope and cost complementarity.
sections.big_idea: In the long run average cost first falls (economies of scale) and then rises (diseconomies of scale); producing two goods together can also be cheaper (economies of scope).
sections.body_md:
**Long-run average cost (LRAC):** the minimum average cost of producing each output when the firm can choose **all** its inputs.

**Economies of scale (LRAC falls as Q rises):** greater **specialisation** and division of labour; better use of **machinery**; **bulk purchasing** and input discounts; **spreading fixed/setup costs** over more units; managerial and technical efficiencies.

**Diseconomies of scale (LRAC rises beyond the optimal scale Q*):** managerial and **coordination** difficulties; **bureaucracy** and slower decisions; difficulty **monitoring** a very large organisation; **congestion** and complexity.

**Multi-product cost function C(Q1, Q2):** the cost of producing two outputs jointly.

- **Economies of scope:** C(Q1, 0) + C(0, Q2) > C(Q1, Q2): cheaper to produce the two jointly than separately.
- **Cost complementarity:** the marginal cost of good 1 **declines** as more of good 2 is produced.

For **C(Q1, Q2) = f + aQ1Q2 + (Q1)² + (Q2)²**: MC1 = aQ2 + 2Q1. **Cost complementarity if a < 0. Economies of scope if f > aQ1Q2.**

visuals.title: The U-shaped LRAC
visuals.caption: Left of Q* average cost falls (economies of scale); right of Q* it rises (diseconomies of scale).

sides.title: Economies of scale
points: Fixed costs spread over more units

sides.title: Diseconomies of scale
points: Hard to monitor a very large organisation

worked.question_md: **The professor's example:** C(Q1, Q2) = 90 - 2Q1Q2 + (Q1)² + (Q2)². Is there cost complementarity? Are there economies of scope?

steps.title: Cost complementarity
steps.body_md: a = -2 < 0, so **yes**. MC1 = aQ2 + 2Q1 = **-2Q2 + 2Q1**: more Q2 lowers MC1.
steps.why: Cost complementarity needs a negative a.

steps.title: Economies of scope
steps.body_md: The rule is f > aQ1Q2. Here aQ1Q2 = -2Q1Q2, which is negative for any positive outputs, and f = 90 is positive, so **f > aQ1Q2: yes**.
steps.why: Joint production saves the fixed cost f.

worked.answer_md: **Yes to both:** a = -2 < 0 gives cost complementarity, and 90 > -2Q1Q2 gives economies of scope.

watch_out: Economies of **scale** are about one product at a bigger size. Economies of **scope** are about two products made **together**.
Cost complementarity needs **a < 0** in front of Q1Q2.
sections.memory_trick: **Scale is size; scope is variety.**
sections.exam_answer_md:
**Economies of scale:** as output rises, LRAC falls (specialisation, better use of machinery, bulk buying, fixed costs spread over more units). **Diseconomies of scale:** beyond the optimal scale Q*, LRAC rises (coordination problems, bureaucracy, monitoring, congestion). So LRAC is U-shaped (draw it, with Q* at the bottom).

**Economies of scope:** C(Q1, 0) + C(0, Q2) > C(Q1, Q2). **Cost complementarity:** the marginal cost of good 1 falls as more of good 2 is produced; with C = f + aQ1Q2 + (Q1)² + (Q2)² this needs a < 0.

sections.title: Trend forecasting by least squares (linear and quadratic)
sections.why: Trend fitting is a full table question (5 marks): build the table, solve two equations, forecast.
sections.big_idea: Fit the straight line S = a + bt through past sales using two normal equations, then put in the future t to forecast.
sections.body_md:
**Linear trend:** S = a + bt, where t numbers the periods 1, 2, 3, and so on.

Find a and b from the two normal equations (the slide's worked example uses exactly these):

- **ΣS = na + bΣt**
- **ΣSt = aΣt + bΣt²**

So the table needs columns **t, t², St** and their sums.

**Straight line or curve?** Look at the differences in sales. Roughly constant **first** differences: straight line. Roughly constant **second** differences: a **quadratic** trend S = a + bt + ct².

For the quadratic, number the years so the middle year is 0 (-3 to 3). Then Σt = 0 and Σt³ = 0, and **b = ΣSt / Σt²** directly.

worked.question_md:
**The professor's question:** assuming the present trend continues, what is the expected sales value for the year 2000?

| Year | 1993 | 1994 | 1995 | 1996 | 1997 |

steps.why: Make the a-terms equal, subtract, and one unknown disappears.

Trend: **S = 594.5 + 53.5t**. The year 2000 is t = 8.

S = 594.5 + 53.5 × 8 = 594.5 + 428 = **1022.5**

sections.title: Elasticity: own price, cross price and income
sections.why: The 2026 mid-term gave 5 marks to price, cross-price and income elasticity in one question; the total revenue test is a regular short question.
sections.big_idea: Elasticity = % change in quantity ÷ % change in the driver; its sign says how they are related and its size says how strongly demand reacts.
sections.body_md:
| Elasticity | Formula | How to read it |
|---|---|---|
| Own price | E(QX,PX) = %ΔQX / %ΔPX | |E| > 1 elastic, |E| < 1 inelastic, |E| = 1 unitary |
| Cross price | E(QX,PY) = %ΔQX / %ΔPY | Positive: substitutes. Negative: complements |
| Income | E(QX,M) = %ΔQX / %ΔM | Positive: normal good. Negative: inferior good |

**Total revenue test:** if demand is **elastic**, price and total revenue move in **opposite** directions; if **inelastic**, they move the **same** way. Total revenue is highest at **unitary** elasticity.

**Demand is more elastic** with more substitutes, over a longer time, and when the good takes a bigger share of the budget.

practice.question_md: **2026 mid-term Q4 (5 marks):** a store sells 500 phones a week at ₹50,000; apps cost ₹100; the average monthly budget is ₹60,000. Find (a) the price elasticity when a discount to ₹45,000 lifts sales to 650; (b) the cross-price elasticity when app prices double to ₹200 and sales drop to 400; (c) the income elasticity when budgets rise to ₹75,000 and sales rise to 700.

steps.title: Price elasticity
steps.why: Each % change is (new - old) ÷ old.

watch_out: Keep the **sign**: for cross and income elasticity the sign is the answer (substitute or complement, normal or inferior).
Elastic means price and revenue move **opposite** ways: a price cut raises revenue.
sections.memory_trick: **Cross: plus means swap (substitutes), minus means pair (complements).**
sections.exam_answer_md: Write the formula, the two % changes with working, the elasticity, and one line of meaning (elastic or inelastic; substitutes or complements; normal or inferior).

sections.title: Equilibrium, surplus, price controls and a tax
sections.why: Both 2026 and 2025 mid-terms asked for equilibrium work and the government's role (price controls, a tax); surplus is a regular 'Explain' question.
sections.big_idea: Equilibrium is where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied; a ceiling below it causes a shortage, a floor above it a surplus, and a tax shifts supply.
sections.body_md:
**Market equilibrium:** the price that balances supply and demand, **Qxs = Qxd**, with no shortage or surplus.

**Consumer surplus:** the value consumers get from a good but do not have to pay for. **Producer surplus:** the amount producers receive in excess of the amount necessary to induce them to produce.

**Government intervention:**

- **Price ceiling** (maximum legal price, below equilibrium): quantity supplied < quantity demanded, a **shortage**. Buyers also pay a nonpecuniary price, so the full economic price is higher.
- **Price floor** (minimum legal price, above equilibrium): quantity demanded < quantity supplied, a **surplus**; the government may buy the surplus.
- **Taxes** are one of the determinants of supply: a tax on producers shifts supply.

sides.title: Price ceiling
points: Full economic price above the ceiling

practice.question_md: **2026 mid-term Q5 (3 marks):** Qd = 300 - 3P and Qs = -60 + 3P. The government puts a specific tax of $10 per unit on producers. Calculate the new price paid by consumers.

steps.title: Equilibrium before the tax
steps.why: Set Qd = Qs first, so you can show the change.

steps.title: Supply after the tax
steps.body_md: Producers keep only P - 10 of each sale, so supply becomes Qs = -60 + 3(P - 10) = **-90 + 3P**.
steps.why: A tax on producers shifts the supply curve.

steps.title: New equilibrium
steps.body_md: 300 - 3P = -90 + 3P, so 390 = 6P and **P = 65**. Consumers pay **$65**; producers keep 55; Q = 105.

practice.answer_md: **Consumers now pay $65 (up from $60); half of the $10 tax falls on consumers here.**

practice.question_md: **The professor's questions:** with Qxd = 400 - 5Px and Qxs = -50 + 5Px, (a) a price ceiling of ₹40: find the shortage; (b) a price floor of ₹50: find the surplus and the cost to the government if it buys it.
practice.answer_md: **Ceiling: shortage of 50. Floor: surplus of 50, costing the government ₹2,500.**

watch_out: A ceiling **below** equilibrium causes a **shortage**; a floor **above** equilibrium causes a **surplus**.
For a tax on producers, replace P with **P - tax** in the supply equation, then solve again.
sections.memory_trick: **Ceiling holds price down, floor holds price up.**
sections.exam_answer_md: **Role of government intervention:** governments can set a **price ceiling** (maximum legal price, below equilibrium, causing a shortage) or a **price floor** (minimum legal price, above equilibrium, causing a surplus), and taxes shift supply. Give one example from the slides for each, then show the effect on a demand and supply diagram.

sections.title: Utility, indifference curves and the budget line
sections.why: Mid-term topics that can return as short questions: MU and TU, consumer equilibrium, the four preference properties, the budget line.
sections.big_idea: A consumer picks the affordable bundle with the highest satisfaction: where the highest reachable indifference curve just touches the budget line (MRS = Px/Py).
sections.body_md:
**Total utility (TU):** the sum of the utilities from all units consumed. **Marginal utility (MU):** the change in TU from one more unit. **Law of diminishing marginal utility:** MU falls as you consume more of a good.

**Budget line:** **PxX + PyY = M**; its intercepts are M/Px and M/Py and its slope is **Px/Py** (in size).

**Four properties of preferences:** completeness, more is better, diminishing marginal rate of substitution, transitivity (so indifference curves do not cross).

**Consumer equilibrium:** the affordable bundle with the highest satisfaction, where **MRS = Px/Py** (the indifference curve's slope equals the budget line's slope).

sides.title: Completeness
points: Every pair of bundles can be ranked

sides.title: Diminishing MRS
points: You give up less and less of Y for each extra X

sides.title: Transitivity
points: C over B and B over A means C over A
So indifference curves do not cross

practice.question_md: **2025 mid-term Q2 (2 marks):** good A costs Rs. 2 and good B Rs. 4; income is Rs. 20. (i) Which bundles lie on the budget line? (ii) How many units of A if all income goes on A? (iii) The budget line's equation? (iv) Its slope?

steps.title: Equation
steps.why: Price times quantity for each good adds up to income.

steps.title: All on A, and the slope
steps.body_md: All income on A: 20/2 = **10 units**. Slope (B on the vertical axis): -2/4 = **-0.5**.

practice.answer_md: **2A + 4B = 20; bundles (10, 0) to (0, 5) as listed; 10 units of A; slope -0.5.**

practice.question_md: **2025 mid-term Q5 (2 marks):** an ice-cream costs Rs. 30. The MU of the 3rd one is 90 utils and the MU of Rs. 1 is 3 utils. Should she eat more or stop?

steps.title: Turn MU into rupees
steps.body_md: 90 utils ÷ 3 utils per rupee = Rs. 30 of satisfaction.

steps.title: Compare with the price
steps.body_md: Rs. 30 of satisfaction = Rs. 30 price, so MU/P equals the MU of money. She is in equilibrium.
steps.why: Equilibrium: MU of the good in money terms equals its price.

practice.answer_md: **She should stop at 3: the 3rd ice-cream's utility is worth exactly its price.**

watch_out: The budget line's slope is the **price ratio**, not the income.
Indifference curves never cross (transitivity).
sections.memory_trick: **Equilibrium = touch:** highest indifference curve touching the budget line.
sections.exam_answer_md: **Consumer equilibrium (indifference curves):** the consumer chooses the affordable bundle with the highest satisfaction, where the highest indifference curve is tangent to the budget line: **MRS = Px/Py**. (Draw it.)

sections.title: Economic profit, present value, perpetuity and NPV
sections.why: The 2026 mid-term had a deferred perpetuity (2 marks) and an NPV choice (5 marks); accounting versus economic profit is a common 3-mark question.
sections.big_idea: Economic profit counts the opportunity cost that accounting profit ignores, and money later is worth less than money now: PV = FV/(1 + i)^n.
sections.body_md:
**Accounting profit** = total revenue - explicit costs. **Economic profit** = total revenue - (explicit + implicit costs): it includes opportunity cost, so it is the complete measure.

**Present value:** PV = FV / (1 + i)^n. **A series:** add the PV of each flow.

**Perpetuity** (pays forever): **PV = CF / i**. If the first payment comes later, CF / i gives the value one period **before** the first payment; then discount that back to today.

**NPV** = PV of future cash flows - the cost today (C₀). Accept if NPV > 0.

practice.question_md: **2026 mid-term Q2 (2 marks):** $800 a year forever, first payment at the end of Year 5, interest 6%. What is its present value today?

steps.title: Value of the perpetuity
steps.body_md: 800 / 0.06 = **$13,333.33**, its value at the end of Year 4 (one period before the first payment).

practice.question_md: **2026 mid-term Q3 (5 marks):** the efficient fridge costs $550 and saves $28 at the end of each of the next 5 years; the standard one costs $420; cost of funds 5%. Which should you buy?

steps.title: Extra cost today
steps.why: Compare only what differs between the two choices.

practice.answer_md: **NPV is negative, so buy the standard model: the savings are worth less today than the extra $130.**

watch_out: A delayed perpetuity: CF/i is the value one period **before** the first payment, so discount for 4 years when the first payment is in Year 5.
NPV compares only the **difference** between options.
sections.memory_trick: **Economic profit pays rent to your alternatives** (it subtracts opportunity cost).
sections.exam_answer_md: **Accounting profit** = TR - explicit costs (ignores opportunity cost). **Economic profit** = TR - (explicit + implicit costs), a complete measure of profitability. Give one example of an implicit cost (the owner's own time or money).
